conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes 'no' to the question of whether saw palmetto improves symptoms of BPH compared to placebo, citing high-quality trial evidence and a Cochrane review showing no superiority over placebo even at higher doses.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: no.** The best placebo-controlled evidence does not show that saw palmetto (*Serenoa repens*) improves urinary symptoms from BPH over the longer term.

Two substantial blinded randomized trials found no advantage over placebo:

- In a 1-year trial of 225 men aged over 49 with moderate-to-severe BPH symptoms, saw-palmetto extract (160 mg twice daily) was **not superior to placebo** for urinary symptoms or objective BPH measures.  
  https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa053085

- A later multicentre randomized placebo-controlled trial assessed escalating doses—up to three times the usual dose—over **72 weeks**. It found no greater symptom reduction than placebo, and no benefit on secondary outcomes. Thus, increasing the dose did not solve the lack of efficacy.  
  https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3326341/

The updated Cochrane systematic-review conclusion is consistent: saw-palmetto monotherapy did not improve lower-urinary-tract symptoms or maximum urinary-flow rate versus placebo, including at double or triple usual doses.  
https://read.qxmd.com/read/22551330/serenoa-repens-monotherapy-for-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia-bph-an-updated-cochrane-systematic-review

This applies to saw palmetto **alone**; findings should not automatically be extrapolated to mixed herbal products, which have separate and more uncertain evidence. Adverse effects in the reviewed evidence were generally mild and similar to placebo.
